cases.title: Margin of error for pain freedom in a migraine trial
cases.context: In a clinical trial, adults with migraine (a recurring headache disorder with throbbing pain, often with nausea) were randomly assigned to take a new drug or a placebo at the start of an attack. The table below shows the number of patients in each group who were pain free 2 hours after the dose. A news report gave the difference between the two groups "plus or minus" a margin of error.
tasks: Find the proportion of patients who were pain free at 2 hours in each group and the difference, Drug minus Placebo.
Calculate the pooled standard error and the 95% margin of error \(z_{0.05}s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\).

What is the 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of pain-free patients between the two treatment groups? Based on the interval, is there evidence that the proportion is different in the two groups?

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of patients who are pain free 2 hours after the dose is the same with the drug and with the placebo.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of patients who are pain free 2 hours after the dose is different with the drug and with the placebo.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (pain-free patients), \(n_i\) (patients in the group), \(\hat p_i\) (sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled proportion), \(s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\) (SE of the difference), \(z_{0.05}\) (two-sided Normal cutoff), \(M\) (margin of error).

steps.title: Find both sample proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the number of pain-free patients divided by the number of patients in that group. Group 1 is the drug and group 2 is the placebo.

steps.title: Find the observed difference
steps.words: Keep the direction Drug minus Placebo throughout. The drug group is about 13 percentage points higher.

steps.title: Pool the two groups
steps.words: Under the null hypothesis both groups share one proportion, so the two groups are pooled to estimate it for the standard error.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: Multiply the pooled variance term by the sum of the reciprocal group sizes, then take the root.

steps.title: Read the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, and use the infinity row in the 0.05 two-tail column. The infinity row gives the standard Normal cutoff, 1.960.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error
steps.words: This product is the number that a report prints after "plus or minus". It is about 9.2 percentage points.

steps.title: Form the interval and decide
steps.words: The interval does not contain 0 because the observed difference is larger than its margin of error. So reject equal proportions at the two-sided 0.05 level.

cases.conclusion: The Drug minus Placebo difference in the proportion of pain-free patients is 13.1 percentage points plus or minus 9.2 points (95% CI 0.0396 to 0.2231). The interval does not contain 0, so there is a difference between the groups (P < 0.05). A larger proportion of patients was pain free at 2 hours with the drug than with the placebo.

cases.title: Padded helmet covers and concussion in football
cases.context: A study was reported concerning concussion (a mild traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head) in high school football. Over one season, 412 players wore a padded cover over the helmet and 530 players wore a standard helmet. The players and their coaches decided who wore the cover, so the groups were not formed by random assignment. The table below shows the number of players in each group who had a diagnosed concussion during the season.
tasks: Use a chi-square test. Is there evidence that the proportion of players with a concussion is different in these two groups? Use a significance level of α = 0.05 for your inference.
Calculate the relative risk of concussion, padded cover group relative to standard helmet group, and interpret it.
Please state what this study can and cannot show, given how the groups were formed.

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of players who have a concussion during the season is the same with a padded cover and with a standard helmet.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of players who have a concussion during the season is different with a padded cover and with a standard helmet.

cases.symbols: \(n_{TD}\) (concussions in the padded cover group), \(n_T\) (padded cover group size), \(n_{CD}\) (concussions in the standard helmet group), \(n_C\) (standard helmet group size), \(O\) (observed count), \(E\) (expected count), \(RR\) (relative risk).

steps.title: Find the group totals
steps.words: Add the players with and without a concussion in each row. The grand total is 942 players, and 62 of them had a concussion.

steps.title: Calculate expected counts
steps.words: Expected counts are what each cell would hold if the proportion of players with a concussion were the same in both groups.

steps.title: Calculate the Yates-corrected chi-square
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference between observed and expected before squaring. This correction is used for 2×2 tables. The first line shows the padded cover and concussion cell, and the other three cells are found the same way.

steps.title: Compare with the chi-square cutoff
steps.words: Open Chi_Squared_Table1.pdf, page 1, row 1. The 0.05 column gives 3.841. The statistic is smaller than this cutoff, so do not reject the null hypothesis (P > 0.05). It is also smaller than the 0.10 cutoff of 2.706 and larger than the 0.25 cutoff of 1.323, so 0.10 < P < 0.25.

steps.title: Calculate both concussion proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the risk of a concussion during the season within that group.

steps.title: Calculate the relative risk
steps.words: In this sample the risk of a concussion in the padded cover group is about 66% of the risk in the standard helmet group.

steps.title: State what the design allows
steps.words: The chi-square test does not reject, so a relative risk this far from 1 could arise by chance with these group sizes. The players also chose their own helmets, so the groups may differ in position, playing time or style of play. Even a significant result would show an association and not a cause. A randomized trial would be needed to show that the cover changes the risk.

cases.conclusion: Do not reject the null hypothesis (chi-square = 2.21, 1 df, 0.10 < P < 0.25). There is no evidence of a difference in the proportion of players with a concussion between the two groups. The relative risk is 0.6589, so in this sample the padded cover group had about 66% of the risk of the standard helmet group, but a difference of this size could arise by chance. The players chose their own helmets, so this study could only show an association and not a cause.

cases.title: Parkinson tremor on years since diagnosis in two treatment groups
cases.context: Researchers interested in resting tremor (an involuntary rhythmic shaking of a limb at rest) in Parkinson disease did a study of two independent groups of patients. Fifteen patients were treated with medication only, and 13 patients were treated with deep brain stimulation (DBS, an implanted electrode that delivers electrical pulses). Tremor amplitude in millimeters (mm) was measured with a wrist accelerometer. For each group, tremor amplitude was regressed on the time since diagnosis in years using R. The table below shows the slope and its standard error from each R output. Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed.
tasks: State the null and alternative hypotheses for the two slopes in symbols and in words.
Calculate the standard error of the difference between the two slopes and the t statistic.

Is there evidence that the trend between tremor amplitude and time since diagnosis is different in these two groups? Give the degrees of freedom, the critical value from the printed t table and a P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: Mean tremor amplitude increases with time since diagnosis at the same rate in patients on medication only and in patients with deep brain stimulation.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which mean tremor amplitude increases with time since diagnosis is different in the two groups of patients.

cases.symbols: \(b_1, b_2\) (sample slopes for medication only and for deep brain stimulation), \(s_{b_1}, s_{b_2}\) (slope standard errors), \(s_{b_1-b_2}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Read both slopes and standard errors
steps.words: Take the slope row of each R coefficient table. The Estimate column gives the slope and the Std. Error column gives its standard error. Group 1 is medication only and group 2 is deep brain stimulation.

steps.title: Calculate the slope difference
steps.words: In these samples tremor amplitude rises about 0.37 mm more per year in the medication-only group than in the deep brain stimulation group.

steps.title: Calculate the SE of the difference
steps.words: The two groups are independent, so the variances of the two slopes add.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Divide the slope difference by its standard error.

steps.title: Find df and the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 24, two-tail 0.05 column. The value is 2.064. Four degrees of freedom are lost because each line estimates an intercept and a slope.

steps.title: Decide and bracket P
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. The statistic is larger than the 0.05 cutoff and the 0.02 cutoff of 2.492, but it is smaller than the 0.01 cutoff of 2.797. So reject equal slopes with 0.01 < P < 0.02.

cases.conclusion: Reject equal slopes (t = 2.561, 24 df, 0.01 < P < 0.02). There is a difference in the trend between tremor amplitude and time since diagnosis in the two groups. Mean tremor amplitude rises faster in the medication-only group (0.6556 mm per year) than in the deep brain stimulation group (0.2854 mm per year).

cases.title: Arm recovery after stroke by matrix least squares
cases.context: The table below shows data on 15 patients who were recovering from a stroke (a loss of blood supply to part of the brain). For each patient the table gives the arm motor score at 12 weeks (y, a clinical movement scale from 0 to 66 points, where a higher score means better movement), the amount of arm therapy in hours per week (h/week) (x1) and the arm motor score at admission (x2). A multiple regression of y on x1 and x2 is fitted with the matrix least-squares formula.
tasks: Build \(X^TX\) and \(X^Ty\) from the sums of the data. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Solve \(b=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\) for \(b_0, b_1, b_2\) and write the fitted equation.
Use \(SS_{res}\) to find \(s_{y|x}\) and \(R^2\).
cases.symbols: \(X\) (design matrix with a column of ones, then x1 and x2), \(y\) (12-week score vector), \(b\) (coefficient vector), \(SS_{res}\) (sum of squared residuals), \(SS_{tot}\) (total sum of squares), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error).

steps.title: Build the cross-product matrix
general: X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}n&\sum x_1&\sum x_2\\\sum x_1&\sum x_1^2&\sum x_1x_2\\\sum x_2&\sum x_1x_2&\sum x_2^2\end{bmatrix}
steps.words: Each entry is a sum over the 15 rows of the table. The first row and the first column come from the column of ones in X, so they hold n and the plain sums.

steps.title: Build the cross-product vector
steps.words: Multiply each column of X by the 12-week score values and add.

steps.title: Invert the cross-product matrix
steps.words: The inverse is found with software. Its diagonal entries are used again for the standard errors of the coefficients.

steps.title: Solve for the coefficients
steps.words: Multiply the inverse by the cross-product vector. R prints the same three numbers in the Estimate column of summary(lm()).

steps.title: Calculate the residual variance
steps.words: Three parameters are estimated, so 12 degrees of freedom remain. The root is the Residual standard error that R prints as 4.246.

steps.title: Calculate R squared
steps.words: About 75% of the variation in the 12-week score is accounted for by therapy time and admission score together. R prints Multiple R-squared 0.7457.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares plane is ŷ = 11.24 + 1.294x1 + 0.7653x2, with s_y|x = 4.246 points on 12 df and R² = 0.7457. These values match the R summary.

cases.title: Overnight word-pair recall by matrix least squares
cases.context: In a study looking at sleep and memory, 12 young adults learned 40 word pairs in the evening and then slept overnight in the laboratory with EEG (electroencephalography, a recording of the electrical activity of the brain from the scalp). The table below shows the number of word pairs recalled the next morning (y), the time spent in slow-wave sleep in minutes (min) (x1) and the sleep spindle density (x2, the number of brief 12 to 15 Hz bursts per minute of light sleep). A multiple regression of y on x1 and x2 is fitted with the matrix least-squares formula.
cases.unit: word pairs per spindle per minute
tasks: Build \(X^TX\) and \(X^Ty\) from the sums of the data. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Solve \(b=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\) for \(b_0, b_1, b_2\) and write the fitted equation.
Use \(SS_{res}\) to find \(s_{y|x}\) and \(R^2\).
cases.symbols: \(X\) (design matrix with a column of ones, then x1 and x2), \(y\) (recall vector), \(b\) (coefficient vector), \(SS_{res}\) (sum of squared residuals), \(SS_{tot}\) (total sum of squares), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error).

steps.title: Build the cross-product matrix
general: X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}n&\sum x_1&\sum x_2\\\sum x_1&\sum x_1^2&\sum x_1x_2\\\sum x_2&\sum x_1x_2&\sum x_2^2\end{bmatrix}
steps.words: Each entry is a sum over the 12 rows of the table. The first row and the first column come from the column of ones in X, so they hold n and the plain sums.

steps.title: Build the cross-product vector
steps.words: Multiply each column of X by the recall values and add.

steps.title: Invert the cross-product matrix
steps.words: The inverse is found with software. Its diagonal entries are used again for the standard errors of the coefficients.

steps.title: Solve for the coefficients
steps.words: Multiply the inverse by the cross-product vector. R prints the same three numbers in the Estimate column of summary(lm()).

steps.title: Calculate the residual variance
steps.words: Three parameters are estimated, so 9 degrees of freedom remain. The root is the Residual standard error that R prints as 1.714.

steps.title: Calculate R squared
steps.words: About 79% of the variation in morning recall is accounted for by slow-wave sleep time and spindle density together. R prints Multiple R-squared 0.7880.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares plane is ŷ = 5.456 + 0.09697x1 + 2.979x2, with s_y|x = 1.714 word pairs on 9 df and R² = 0.7880. These values match the R summary.

cases.title: Reading the R summary for cigarette craving
cases.context: A study was reported concerning cigarette craving in 24 daily smokers. Each subject viewed smoking-related images (cue exposure) and then rated the urge to smoke on a 100-point craving scale (0 = no urge, 100 = strongest urge). Craving ("Craving"; points on the craving scale) is the dependent variable; nicotine dependence score ("Dependence"; a questionnaire score from 0 to 10) and time since the last cigarette ("Hours"; hours) are the independent variables. We are interested in investigating if these measures can "explain" craving. The R call lm(Craving ~ Dependence + Hours) printed the summary below.
tasks: Based on the R results, show how you would reject the null hypothesis of no relation between craving and all of the variables above (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero). Provide the alternate hypothesis as part of your answer. Recompute F from \(R^2\) and give the critical value from the printed F table.
Based on the R results, which explanatory variables are statistically significant? Use \(t=b_j/s_{b_j}\) with the printed t table and give the 95% confidence interval for each slope.
Estimate the craving score of a smoker that has a dependence score of 6 and smoked the last cigarette 8 hours ago.

hypotheses.nullWords: Neither the nicotine dependence score nor the time since the last cigarette is related to the mean craving score.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: At least one of the two variables is related to the mean craving score.

cases.symbols: \(R^2\) (multiple R-squared), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(n\) (number of smokers), \(MS_{mod}, MS_{res}\) (model and residual mean squares), \(b_j\) (coefficient), \(s_{b_j}\) (its standard error).

steps.title: Find the F degrees of freedom
steps.words: Two independent variables are tested together, so 21 degrees of freedom remain for the residuals.

steps.title: Recompute F from R squared
steps.words: Dividing SS_mod and SS_res by SS_tot turns them into R² and 1 − R², so F can be checked from the printed R². R prints 22.71.

steps.title: Compare with the F cutoff
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, page 1, numerator column 2, denominator row 21. The lightface value is 3.47 and the boldface value is 5.78. F is larger than both, so reject the null hypothesis of no relation with P < 0.01 from the table. R prints P = 5.613e-06.

steps.title: Test the dependence coefficient
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 21. The 0.05 column gives 2.080. The statistic is also larger than 3.819, the 0.001 cutoff, so P < 0.001. R prints 5.60e-06.

steps.title: Test the hours coefficient
steps.words: The hours coefficient is also significant, but less strongly. The statistic lies between 2.080 (0.05) and 2.518 (0.02), so 0.02 < P < 0.05. R prints 0.0315.

steps.title: Build 95% intervals for both slopes
steps.words: Neither interval contains 0, which agrees with both t tests. The lower end of the Hours interval is close to 0, which matches its P value near 0.03.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute a dependence score of 6 and 8 hours into the fitted equation. The result is a mean craving score on the 100-point scale.

cases.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis of no relation (F = 22.71 on 2 and 21 df, P < 0.01 from the printed table and P = 5.613e-06 from R). Dependence and Hours together predict craving. Dependence is significant (t = 6.024, P < 0.001) and Hours is significant (t = 2.304, 0.02 < P < 0.05). The estimated mean craving score of a smoker with a dependence score of 6 and 8 hours since the last cigarette is 53.2 points.

cases.title: Speech in noise with summary, confint, refit and prediction
cases.context: Researchers interested in the understanding of speech in background noise did a study of 30 older adults. Each subject repeated sentences that were presented in multi-talker babble (a recording of several people talking at once), and the score was the percentage of keywords repeated correctly. Speech-in-noise score ("Score"; % of keywords correct) is the dependent variable; age ("Age"; years), pure-tone average hearing threshold ("PTA"; the mean threshold at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz in decibels hearing level, dB HL) and musical training ("Music"; years) are the independent variables. R printed the summary(), the confint() output and a second summary() after the analysis was re-done with only the explanatory variables that were statistically significant.
tasks: Write the full regression equation. Based on the R results, show how you would reject the null hypothesis of no relation between the score and all of the variables above (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero).

Based on the R results, which explanatory variables are statistically significant? Based on the confint() confidence intervals, make an inference about the significance of each explanatory variable. Do these results agree with your conclusions from the t tests?

Using the resulting regression equation (the analysis re-done with only the explanatory variables that were statistically significant), estimate the score of a 70-year-old listener that has a pure-tone average of 30 dB HL. You can do this calculation by-hand.

hypotheses.nullWords: Years of musical training have no relation to the mean speech-in-noise score once age and pure-tone average are in the model.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Years of musical training are related to the mean speech-in-noise score once age and pure-tone average are in the model.

cases.symbols: \(b_j\) (coefficient estimate), \(s_{b_j}\) (standard error), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(\nu=n-k-1\) (residual degrees of freedom), \(\hat y\) (predicted mean score).

steps.title: Write the full equation
steps.words: Read the Estimate column of the full summary. The mean score is lower at an older age and at a higher (worse) pure-tone average.

steps.title: Test the model as a whole
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, page 1, numerator column 3, denominator row 26. The lightface value is 2.98 and the boldface value is 4.64. F is larger than both, so reject the null hypothesis that all three coefficients are zero (P < 0.01). R prints P = 1.823e-08.

steps.title: Test each coefficient
steps.words: Compare each magnitude with t_0.05(26) = 2.056 (t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 26). Age and PTA are larger than 2.056 and also larger than 3.707, the 0.001 cutoff, so P < 0.001 for each. Music is smaller than 2.056 (R prints P = 0.228), so Music is not statistically significant. The by-hand t for Age differs from the R value of -5.784 in the last digit because R divides the unrounded numbers.

steps.title: Confirm with the 95% intervals
steps.words: The by-hand Music interval matches confint() to rounding. It contains 0, while the Age and PTA intervals do not, which agrees with the t tests.

steps.title: Refit without Music
steps.words: The refitted coefficients change slightly because Music no longer shares the explanation. Both remaining t values (-5.681 and -4.263 on 27 df) are larger in magnitude than 3.690, the 0.001 cutoff, so P < 0.001. R² falls only from 0.7705 to 0.757.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute age 70 and a pure-tone average of 30 dB HL into the refitted equation. The result is a mean score in percent of keywords correct.

cases.conclusion: The model as a whole is significant (F = 29.09 on 3 and 26 df, P < 0.01). Age and PTA are significant (P < 0.001) but Music is not (t = 1.233, and its interval contains 0). The refitted model is ŷ = 113.93698 − 0.50150·Age − 0.51302·PTA, and the estimated mean score of a 70-year-old listener with a pure-tone average of 30 dB HL is 63.44%.

cases.title: Reading the R summary for cold pressor pain tolerance
cases.context: In a study looking at pain tolerance, 35 healthy adults held one hand in ice water (the cold pressor test), and the tolerance time in seconds (s) until the hand was withdrawn was recorded. Tolerance time ("Tolerance"; seconds) is the dependent variable; trait anxiety score ("Anxiety"; a questionnaire score from 20 to 80), sleep duration on the previous night ("Sleep"; hours) and pain catastrophizing score ("Catastrophizing"; a questionnaire score from 0 to 52 that measures how strongly a person magnifies and dwells on pain) are the independent variables. The R call lm(Tolerance ~ Anxiety + Sleep + Catastrophizing) printed the summary below.
tasks: Based on the R results, show how you would reject the null hypothesis of no relation between tolerance time and all of the variables above (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero). Provide the alternate hypothesis as part of your answer. Recompute F from \(R^2\) and give the critical value from the printed F table.
Based on the R results, which explanatory variables are statistically significant? Use \(t=b_j/s_{b_j}\) with the printed t table and give the 95% confidence interval for each slope.
Estimate the tolerance time of a subject that has an anxiety score of 45, slept 7.5 hours and has a catastrophizing score of 20.

hypotheses.nullWords: None of the three variables (anxiety score, sleep duration, catastrophizing score) is related to the mean tolerance time.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: At least one of the three variables is related to the mean tolerance time.

cases.symbols: \(R^2\) (multiple R-squared), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(MS_{mod}, MS_{res}\) (model and residual mean squares), \(b_j\) (coefficient), \(s_{b_j}\) (its standard error).

steps.title: Find the F degrees of freedom
steps.words: Three independent variables are tested together, so 31 degrees of freedom remain for the residuals.

steps.title: Recompute F from R squared
steps.words: Dividing SS_mod and SS_res by SS_tot turns them into R² and 1 − R², so F can be checked from the printed R². R prints 12.68.

steps.title: Compare with the F cutoff
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, page 1, numerator column 3. The table has no row for 31 denominator degrees of freedom, so use the nearest smaller printed row, 30. Its cutoffs are slightly larger than the exact ones, so the comparison is conservative. The lightface value is 2.92 and the boldface value is 4.51. F is larger than both, so reject the null hypothesis of no relation with P < 0.01 from the table. R prints P = 1.408e-05.

steps.title: Test the anxiety coefficient
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 31. The 0.05 column gives 2.040. The magnitude lies between 3.375 (0.002) and 3.633 (0.001), so 0.001 < P < 0.002. R prints 0.00100, a value just above 0.001 after rounding.

steps.title: Test the sleep coefficient
steps.words: The sleep coefficient is significant. The statistic is larger than 3.633, the 0.001 cutoff, so P < 0.001. R prints 0.000153.

steps.title: Test the catastrophizing coefficient
steps.words: The catastrophizing coefficient is significant at 0.05, but only just short of the next cutoff. The magnitude lies between 2.040 (0.05) and 2.453 (0.02), so 0.02 < P < 0.05. R prints 0.0203. R shows a t value of -2.446 because it divides the unrounded numbers.

steps.title: Build 95% intervals for the slopes
steps.words: None of the three intervals contains 0, which agrees with the three t tests. The Anxiety and Catastrophizing intervals are entirely negative, and the Sleep interval is entirely positive.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute an anxiety score of 45, 7.5 hours of sleep and a catastrophizing score of 20 into the fitted equation. The result is a mean tolerance time in seconds.

cases.conclusion: Reject the null hypothesis of no relation (F = 12.68 on 3 and 31 df, P < 0.01 from the printed table with row 30 and P = 1.408e-05 from R). All three explanatory variables are statistically significant. Mean tolerance time is shorter at a higher anxiety score (0.001 < P < 0.002) and at a higher catastrophizing score (0.02 < P < 0.05), and it is longer with more sleep (P < 0.001). The estimated mean tolerance time of a subject with an anxiety score of 45, 7.5 hours of sleep and a catastrophizing score of 20 is 92.7 s.

cases.title: Probability and odds of alcohol dependence by age at first drink
cases.context: A study was reported concerning the age at which a person first drank alcohol and alcohol dependence (a pattern of drinking with loss of control and withdrawal symptoms) in adulthood. For 120 adults, the age at the first drink in years (AgeFirst) and the presence of alcohol dependence by age 30 (Dependence, 1 = present, 0 = absent) were recorded. R fitted glm(Dependence ~ AgeFirst, family = "binomial") by maximum likelihood and printed the coefficient table below.
tasks: Based on the z value for AgeFirst, is the age at the first drink related to the probability of alcohol dependence?
Estimate the probability of alcohol dependence of an adult that had the first drink at age 14.
Fill in the blank. The odds of alcohol dependence for an adult who had the first drink at age 14 are __ : 1.

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability of alcohol dependence does not change with the age at the first drink.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability of alcohol dependence changes with the age at the first drink.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (age at the first drink in years), \(p\) (probability of alcohol dependence), \(z\) (estimate divided by its standard error).

steps.title: Test the age coefficient
steps.words: Use the infinity row of t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, for the Normal cutoffs. They are 1.960 at 0.05 and 3.2905 at 0.001. The magnitude is larger than both, so reject the null hypothesis with P < 0.001. R prints 0.000169.

steps.title: Form the linear predictor
steps.words: The linear predictor is the logit, the natural log of the odds. It is negative here, so the probability is below one half.

steps.title: Convert to a probability
steps.words: The logistic function keeps the result between 0 and 1. Rounded to two places, p = 0.40.

steps.title: Calculate the odds
steps.words: Dividing the rounded probability 0.40 by 0.60 gives 0.67. Carrying the linear predictor without rounding gives 0.65, which is the more accurate value. Odds below 1 mean that dependence is less likely than not for this person.

cases.conclusion: The age at the first drink is a significant predictor of alcohol dependence (z = -3.762, P < 0.001). The negative coefficient means that the probability of dependence falls as the age at the first drink rises. An adult who had the first drink at age 14 has an estimated probability of dependence of 0.3954 (0.40), and the odds are about 0.65 to 1 (0.67 to 1 from the rounded probability).

cases.title: Tone detection and sound level
cases.context: In a hearing experiment, one listener was tested with a 1 kHz tone at 12 sound levels from 10 to 32 decibels sound pressure level (dB SPL), with two trials at each level in random order. On each of the 24 trials the listener reported whether the tone was heard (Heard, 1 = yes, 0 = no). R fitted glm(Heard ~ Level, family = "binomial") and printed the coefficient table below.
tasks: Based on the R output, is the sound level related to the probability that the tone is heard?
Estimate the probability that the tone is heard at 16 dB SPL and at 30 dB SPL.
Calculate the factor by which the odds of hearing the tone change for each 1 dB increase in level.

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability that the tone is heard does not change with the sound level.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability that the tone is heard changes with the sound level.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (sound level, dB SPL), \(p\) (probability that the tone is heard), \(e^{b_1}\) (odds multiplier per decibel).

steps.title: Test the level coefficient
steps.words: The statistic is just larger than the 0.05 Normal cutoff (t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, infinity row) but smaller than the 0.02 cutoff, so 0.02 < P < 0.05. R prints 0.0470.

steps.title: Probability at 16 dB SPL
steps.words: At this quiet level the estimated probability that the tone is heard is about 0.20.

steps.title: Probability at 30 dB SPL
steps.words: A louder tone has a much higher estimated probability of being heard, about 0.67. The fitted probability is one half where the linear predictor is 0, at 25.2 dB SPL.

steps.title: Odds multiplier per decibel
steps.words: Each 1 dB increase multiplies the odds of hearing the tone by about 1.163, a 16% increase in the odds.

cases.conclusion: The sound level is a significant predictor of hearing the tone (z = 1.986, 0.02 < P < 0.05). The estimated probability that the tone is heard is 0.199 at 16 dB SPL and 0.672 at 30 dB SPL, and the odds of hearing the tone rise by a factor of 1.163 per decibel.

questions.stem: In the migraine trial (87 of 210 patients on the drug and 58 of 205 patients on the placebo were pain free at 2 hours), what is the 95% margin of error for the difference in proportions, using the pooled standard error?
questions.why: The margin is 1.960 times the pooled standard error 0.04681, which is 0.0918. The other values are the standard error alone, or the standard error times the 0.10 cutoff 1.6449 or the 0.01 cutoff 2.5758.

questions.stem: In the helmet study (21 of 412 players with a padded cover and 41 of 530 players with a standard helmet had a concussion), what is the relative risk of concussion for the padded cover group?
questions.why: RR divides the padded cover proportion 0.05097 by the standard helmet proportion 0.07736. Inverting the ratio, dividing the raw counts, or using the odds ratio gives the other values.

questions.stem: For the Parkinson tremor comparison (medication only, slope 0.6556 with SE 0.1223, and deep brain stimulation, slope 0.2854 with SE 0.0771), what is the t statistic for equal slopes?
questions.why: t = 0.3702/0.14457 = 2.561. The other values add the two standard errors without squaring, test one slope against zero, or forget the square root.

questions.stem: For the stroke arm recovery regression (15 patients, two independent variables, \(SS_{res}=216.295\)), what is the residual standard error \(s_{y|x}\)?
questions.why: Divide SS_res by n − k − 1 = 12 and take the root, which gives 4.246. Stopping at the variance, or dividing by n − 1 = 14 or by n = 15, gives the other values.

questions.stem: The cigarette craving summary prints Multiple R-squared 0.6838 for 24 smokers and two explanatory variables. What is the F statistic for the null hypothesis of no relation?
questions.why: F = (R²/k)/((1 − R²)/(n − k − 1)) with k = 2 and n − k − 1 = 21, which gives 22.71. Leaving out both degrees of freedom, leaving out k, or using n − 1 = 23 gives the other values.

questions.stem: The alcohol dependence model has \(b_0=3.57133\) and \(b_1=-0.28544\) per year of age at the first drink. What is the estimated probability of dependence for a first drink at age 14?
questions.why: The linear predictor is -0.42483, and p = 1/(1 + e^(0.42483)) = 0.3954. The other values come from the wrong sign in the exponent, from stopping at the odds, or from reading the linear predictor as a probability.

questions.stem: Hippocampal volume is regressed on age, years of education and hours of weekly exercise in 60 older adults. In the R summary the F-statistic line has a p-value below 0.001, the Age and Exercise rows have Pr(>|t|) below 0.01, and the Education row has Pr(>|t|) = 0.41. What is the correct reading?
options: The whole model is not significant, because one of its variables is not significant.
Education must stay in the model, because the F test for the model is significant.
The model as a whole is related to hippocampal volume, but education adds no significant information once age and exercise are in the model, so the model can be refitted without it.
Education is not correlated with age or with exercise.
questions.why: The F test asks whether all coefficients are zero together, and each t test asks whether one variable adds information given the others. A variable with a large P value can be dropped and the model refitted with the significant variables.

questions.stem: For 80 patients with epilepsy, a neurologist records whether each patient has a seizure in the month after a change of medication (yes or no) and the blood level of the drug. Which analysis relates the probability of a seizure to the blood level?
options: Logistic regression, with glm(Seizure ~ Level, family = "binomial").
Simple linear regression of the yes or no outcome on the blood level, with lm().
A paired t test on the blood levels.
A chi-square test on the mean blood level.
questions.why: The outcome is yes or no, so its probability is modeled with the logistic function, which stays between 0 and 1. A straight line fitted to a yes or no outcome can predict values below 0 or above 1.

questions.stem: Among stroke survivors, the patients who chose to join a music therapy program had a lower proportion of depression diagnoses over the next year than the patients who did not join (relative risk 0.70, chi-square test P < 0.01). What does this study show?
options: Music therapy prevents 30% of the cases of depression after a stroke.
Joining the program is associated with a lower risk of depression, but the patients chose their own group, so the study cannot show that the program caused the lower risk.
Nothing, because a relative risk below 1 can never be statistically significant.
Patients with depression are 70% more likely to join the program.
questions.why: The groups were formed by choice and not by random assignment, so they may differ in other ways such as stroke severity or family support. A significant relative risk then shows an association only.

questions.stem: Reaction time is regressed on blood alcohol concentration separately in 12 young adults and in 14 older adults, and the two slopes are compared with a t test. How many degrees of freedom does the test use?
questions.why: Each regression line estimates an intercept and a slope, so four degrees of freedom are lost in total. ν = 12 + 14 − 4 = 22.

notes: All data are invented. Every regression and logistic model was fitted with statsmodels from the raw data stored in check_session19a.py, and the tables carry the fitted numbers rounded the way R prints them (Estimate and Std. Error to a common number of decimals, t and z to 3 decimals, P values to 3 significant digits, Residual SE, R-squared and F to 4 significant digits). The output was not produced by R itself.

R output is carried in `table` exactly as the reference cases do it (coefficient rows plus one last summary row, and an Output column for the summary, confint and refit case). Step lookups use the key `classTable`, as in the reference file.

n19-cold-pressor-summary has 31 residual degrees of freedom. F_table.pdf has no denominator row 31, so the solution uses the printed row 30 (2.92 and 4.51), which is conservative, and the lookup is flagged approximation true with actualDf 31. The t table does print row 31.

n19-cold-pressor-summary lands close to two cutoffs. |t| for Anxiety is 3.632 against the 0.001 cutoff 3.633 (R prints P = 0.00100), and |t| for Catastrophizing is 2.447 against the 0.02 cutoff 2.453.

By-hand t values use the printed (rounded) estimates and standard errors, as in the reference cases, so two of them differ from the R t value in the last digit (Age in the speech case, -5.785 against -5.784, and Catastrophizing in the cold pressor case, -2.447 against -2.446). The solutions say so.

n19-helmet-concussion-risk does not reject (Yates chi-square 2.21 < 3.841). n19-tone-detection-level is just past the 0.05 Normal cutoff (z = 1.986). n19-speech-noise-refit is the case where one variable (Music) is not significant and the model is refitted without it.

The logistic cases keep the reference value keys because the logistic board reads them. In n19-first-drink-dependence, `age` is the age at the first drink and `oddsSlide` is the odds from the probability rounded to two places. In n19-tone-detection-level, `p16` and `p30` are the probabilities at 16 and 30 dB SPL, `oddsPerDegree` is the odds multiplier per decibel and `halfwayTemp` is the level where the fitted probability is one half.
The slopes case keeps the reference keys bM, sbM, nM (medication only) and bF, sbF, nF (deep brain stimulation), while the symbols shown to the student are b_1 and b_2.
The odds task uses the requested wording "are __ : 1", which is the only colon in a task. Everywhere else odds are written as "to 1".
Both multiple-regression fit cases were given positive slopes because the fit board draws the coefficient bars from zero.

Style review: the three R-summary cases now state the variables in the homework's own form ("Name"; unit) is the dependent variable; ... are the independent variables, and their tasks carry his wording (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero). These are the only semicolons in context and tasks, and check_session19a.py allows colons and semicolons there.
